newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK businessmen applaud Albright on China's MFN.
newsitem.headline: HK businessmen applaud Albright on China's MFN.

text.p: Hong Kong's business sector on Wednesday applauded the verbal support of U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright for an extension of China's trade privileges, saying the remarks could improve the chance of renewal.
"I think we have to welcome that sort of support," Jeffrey Muir, vice chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, told Reuters.

On Tuesday, Albright argued a case for a renewal of China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading privileges when she addressed the U.S. Congress, which will decide whether to overturn President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's status for another year.
Albright mentioned Hong Kong in her speech, noting a removal of China's MFN would affect the territory's economy.

"I think Mrs Albright's speech is helpful because it's important that our (U.S.) government leaders come out and support the administration's policy," Muir said, adding that her comments could influence Congress members who had been undecided on the issue.
"I think in this particular year, with all the changes that are going on in Hong Kong, it's even more important that we have extension of MFN," he said.
A loss of China's MFN status could undermine confidence in Hong Kong, now preparing for its return to Chinese rule on July 1, businessmen say.

"We feel that this annual exercise of MFN is not conducive to the maintenance of confidence in the future of the region or indeed of Hong Kong," said Christopher Hammerbeck, executive director of the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's business community has been urging for a perpetual MFN status for China instead of an annual renewal.
They generally expect an extension of China's MFN this year.
"We are cautiously optimistic," Hammerbeck said.
But Muir warned the vote in the Congress would be less supportive of the extension as it was last year.
"It would be somewhat naive on our part not to see that the opposition again is growing to MFN extension and so the question is what about future years," he said.
The territory serves as an entrepot for China, and many Hong Kong manufacturers have moved their production bases to China to take advantage of lower production costs.

Hong Kong's government has said a withdrawal of China's MFN status might slash about HK$174 billion (US$22 billion) to HK$ 246 billion (US$32 billion) from the territory's overall trade, cut Hong Kong's gross domestic product growth by two to 2.8 percentage points, and lead to a loss of 61,000 to 86,000 jobs.
"Obviously those costs would be significant for Hong Kong and it would be something that would hurt our economy," Muir said.
The territory would take the greatest blow should China's MFN status be revoked, he said.
"The entity that would be most hurt by that would be Hong Kong, perhaps even more hurt than China, mainland China, and more than the United States," Muir said.
"Hong Kong has had the unique role of really being an entrepot, middleman, in the U.S.-China trading relationship. And so it is a very, very significant component of our business here," he said.
"Hong Kong's economy is not as broad-based as China's or the United States' and is more vulnerable to this sort of situation."
Hammerbeck warned that a withdrawal of China's trading privileges would also affect global players with investment in China.
